gap, the legislative gap, that was left be hind after the 9 years that the Labour-Green
Government failed to even consider it—along with a lot of other things it failed to
consider, like water. This Government is not afraid to deal with the hard issues. Today
we have brought to the House a bill that not  only is widely supported in the community
but has been given approval by the Parliame ntary Commissioner fo r the Environment,
whose opinion I do value.
This bill is not about pitting the ec onomy against the environment; it is about
responsible management of our  oceans. In clause 11, the bill gives effect to our
obligations under the United Nations Conventi on on the Law of the Sea to manage and
protect the natural resources we have in th e exclusive economic zone. It is worth noting
also that the United Nations Convention on th e Law of the Sea provides coastal States
like New Zealand with exclusive rights over  all resources in th e exclusive economic
zone, while preserving pre-existing navi gational rights—and that means peaceful
passage—and other rights in these areas. So the United Nations Convention on the Law
of the Sea is quite a wide agreement that we are giving effect to in this bill.
The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea sets rules for activities like the
conduct of scientific resear ch, and it also gives effect  to duties regarding the
management and conservation of fisher ies and the protection of the marine
environment. The Environmental Protection Authority will be the decision maker for all
consents, and all consent applications will be decided by that body within a statutory
time frame of 6 months for the marine cons ent process. It was interesting that the
previous but one speaker, Rino Tirikatene, from the Labour benches, thinks it is good to
look at these applications on a case by case basis. Well, yes, it is. The good news for
that member is that the Environmental Pr otection Authority is the body that will be
considering those applications.
Although the bill sets up the general framework for the regulatory system, specific
controls and standards will be set out in  subsequent regulation. There will be a
transitional period enabling planned activ ities to proceed in the 2013-14 season.
Regional councils will still be responsible under the Resource Management Act for
regional coastal plans and consenting activities for up to 12 nautical miles offshore.
The Exclusive Economic Zone and Continen tal Shelf (Environmental Effects) Bill
does not intend—never did intend—to be the Resource Management Act of the seas.
The Resource Management Act was designed for predominantly la nd-based activities.
Although this bill has adopted a similar purpose clause to that of the Resource
Management Act—thanks to a good Minist er who was prepared to listen to
submissions—there are several reasons for a slightly different legislative approach. First
of all, the definition of “environment” is na rrower in the bill than it is in the Resource
Management Act. The Resource Management Act refers to physical resources like
buildings and roads, and also refers to people, communities, and things like amenity
values and social conditions. The Exclus ive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf
(Environmental Effects) Bill definition of “environment” refers only to the marine
28 Aug 2012 EEZ & Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Bill 4803
natural environment, including its ecosystem s. There is a fundamental difference on
that, which seems to have escaped the Labour members.
Secondly, there are our intern ational obligations, particularly those under the United
Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. The United Nations Convention on the Law
of the Sea grants New Zealand limited sove reign rights and sets  limits on what the
Crown can regulate. For example, the Crown has very limited abilities to interfere in
marine scientific research carried out by foreign-flag sh ips. Clearly, the Resource
Management Act has not got sovereignty over this part of it, so the Exclusive Economic
Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Bill has to provide for these
activities to be permitted in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law
of the Sea. Because the rules are set out in the United Nations Convention on the Law
of the Sea, the use of the Resource Manageme nt Act framework is clearly inappropriate
in these activities.
The exclusive economic zone area of ocean  is 20 times New Zealand’s land area and
offers us significant economic opportunities, but  we must also ensure that we have
robust laws in place to protect the envir onment. The Exclusive Economic Zone and
Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Bi ll does just that, and I commend it to the
House. Thank you.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Exclusive Economic Zone and
Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Bill be now read a third time.

NATIONAL WAR MEMORIAL PARK (PUKEAHU) EMPOWERING BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.role: Minist er for Arts, Culture and Heritage

items.text: I move, That the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill be now read
a first time.  I intend that it be referred to th e Transport and Industrial Relations
Committee. At the appropriate time I am going to move that the National War Memorial
Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill be reported  to the House by 18 September, and that
the committee have authority to meet at a ny time while the House is sitting, except
during oral questions, during an y evening on a day on which th ere has been a sitting of
the House, and on a Friday in a week in wh ich there has been a sitting of the House,
despite Standing Orders 188 and 191(1)(b) and (c).
On 7 August the Prime Minister announced th e Government’s intention to create a
National War Memorial Park in front of th e National War Memorial. New legislation is
required to give effect to Cabinet’s decisions and to enable this work to be completed in
time for the centenary commemorations of the Gallipoli landings on Anzac Day 2015.
Before I outline the provisions of the bill, it is very important to remember why the
memorial was erected, and to acknowledge how  the current precinct falls short of the
original vision. In the First World War over 100,000 New Zealanders served overseas.
This would be an astonishing commitmen t today from a population of 4.5 million, let
alone from the 1914 population of just over 1 million people. A total of 18,500
servicemen and servicewomen lost their live s, and we can only imagine now the depth
4804 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
of grief across every community in this c ountry, let alone the challenges facing the
families of the nearly 50,000 wounded who returned.
So in 1919 the Government of William Ferguson Massey decided that a National
War Memorial should be erected so that future generations would remember this
enormous sacrifice. It was de cided that the memorial should be erected on a site with a
commanding position, so that it could be seen from many points in the city and from the
harbour. The Pukeahu site on Buckle Street met those criteria. The term “Puke-ahu” is
the ancient Māori name for that particular ridge. In fact, over a decade passed before the
memorial was finally opened in 1932. Fifty thousand people were there to hear the
national Carillon bells ring for the first time.
A grand boulevard from the memorial to the sea had been included in the plans, but
this never eventuated. In my opinion th at was a good thing, too, because I always
thought it looked as th ough it had been designed by Albe rt Speer. The planned Hall of
Memories was thwarted by the onset of the Depression and the Second World War, and
it was not completed until 1964. The Tomb of the Unknown Warrior was added in
2004. These developments all complement th e 1919 vision, but the setting clearly does
not. In particular, State Highway 1 is incompatible with the memorial’s status as a place
of quiet contemplation and reflection wher e families, dignitaries, and visitors can
honour the service of our forebears. Quite apart from the constant noise of traffic, there
simply is not enough space immediately in front of the memorial for the ever-increasing
number of New Zealanders who come toge ther to remember the fallen on Anzac Day
and other important occasions in  the life of our country. With  the centenary of the First
World War approaching, it is time to address these issues.
The project made possible by this legislation will dive rt the traffic underground and
unite the different sections of the memorial  precinct for the first time. The Anzac Day
commemorations in 2015 will take place in a new, open space flanked on either side by
landscaped areas with trees, seating, cyclew ays, and walking path s. The new park is
also going to provide an appropriate setti ng for an Australian memorial, which is
planned to complement the existing Ne w Zealand memorial in Canberra. Other
memorials will be added over time, and there will be an interpretation centre, which will
provide information to those who come here to reflect on the sacrifices of those who
served their country. Un der the existing statutory processe s, it would not be possible to
guarantee the completion of the project within the required time frame.
What I want to do is just briefly outline the very extensive consultation that has taken
place with the community and with affected  parties about the memorial park over a
number of years, because it shows why we ar e able to fast track this matter. Since 2008
I have consulted over the years with the Port Nicholson Block Settlement Trust, Mount
Cook residents, the local Mt Cook Prim ary School, the National War Memorial
Advisory Council, Massey University, th e Wellington City Council, the Royal New
Zealand Returned and Services’ Association, and the regional council. I have to say that
the response was positive—indeed, universally  positive. What consultation with the
community made clear, when I became the Mini ster, was that the original plan for the
park, which involved the option of moving State Highway 1—that section of Buckle
Street—back away from the memorial and cl oser to the children’s playground, was not
acceptable. I have always been very concerne d about the welfare of the children at Mt
Cook School. With the passage of this bill, stage one of the development can
commence. This will see State Highway 1 temporarily diverted northwards. The
undergrounding work will begin in early 2013, and landscaping in late 2014.
I want to acknowledge the assistance of th e Prime Minister a nd the Minister of
Transport in achieving this outcome. On ce again, they have gone in to bat for
Wellington. Two years ago they intervened to save the Hobbit movies in this country,
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4805
and they have once again brought their considerable vision to this project to ensure there
are no corners cut and no halfway measures as  we develop a memorial park that the
soldiers deserve. This would not have ha ppened without Gerry Brownlee’s support, and
I salute him. He is a wonderful collea gue. Secondly, I acknowledge Sandy McCallum,
the Principal of Mt Cook School, who has b een a tireless advocate for the children
under her care and has helped us to this be st result. Finally, I acknowledge the Deputy
Mayor of Wellington, Ian McKinnon. He and I ha ve worked closely on this project for
years to get the best outcome for the city.
The bill will empower the creation of a National War Me morial Park, providing the
certainty necessary for its completion by Anzac Day 2015 while ensuring the
integration of the park and roading networ ks within the wider city of Wellington. The
bill will grant the statutory authorisations and property rights necessary to complete the
roading and landscaping in time for th at important centennial event. These
authorisations are necessary  to complete the park on time and to avoid, remedy, or
mitigate any actual or potential adverse effects on the environment. It requires the
Transport Agency and the Ministry for Culture  and Heritage to comply with existing
social and environmental responsibilities and expectations.
Subpart 6 of Part 2 gives the Governor-General authority by Order in Council, on the
recommendation of the relevant Minister, to grant additional authorisations and rights,
or to amend authorisations and rights gran ted by the bill, if reasonably necessary or
desirable for the purposes of the Act. The en actments that may be the subject of an
Order in Council are listed under clause 24(2)  of the bill, and clauses 26 and 27 provide
for a National War Memorial Park Review Panel to provide advice in relation to Orders
in Council that may be requ ired. Subpart 7 requires the Minister to arrange for a
community forum of at least 20 people to pr ovide advice in relation to the development
of the park, and the bill stipul ates relevant stakeholders to be represented at that forum.
The provisions relating to Orders in Counc il and the removal of appeal and objection
rights will expire at the close of play on 31 July 2015.
In conclusion, this legislation has been dr afted for a very specific purpose, and will
deliver a result that I believe that all New Z ealanders will be proud of. I believe that we
are all agreed that the National War Memori al should be one of the most solemn and
sacred places in this country. In 1919 the National War Memorial was approved without
a single voice of dissent in this House. It was a matter that was above politics. I hope
there will be similar broad support for this bill in 2012.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I am pleased to speak on the
National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Em powering Bill, and I begin by saying that
my colleague Grant Robertson,  the Wellington Central member  of Parliament, is sorry
that he could not be here to speak in the first reading, but, unfortunately, family issues
take priority today. But as another Wellingt on member of Parliament and a person
involved in the original idea in the last La bour Government, I am very pleased to be
able to speak on this bill. We will support this bill, and we will work with the
Government to ensure its passage. We do ha ve some amendments that we would like
considered at the Transport and Industrial Re lations Committee. I will talk more about
them in a moment.
The National War Memorial Park will be situ ated adjacent to the site of the existing
National War Memorial, the Carillon, and the Ha ll of Memories, as has been defined in
the National War Memorial Act 1992. The esta blishment of a National War Memorial
Park is the policy of the prev ious Labour Government. I have to say that it was a very
strong vision of the former  Prime Minister Helen Clar k. In 2004 Helen Clark, after
several years of negotiating and planning, le d the return of th e Unknown Warrior to
New Zealand and the formal burial of the remains at the memorial. It was her passion
4806 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
that New Zealand would have a resting place to represent the thousands of New Zealand
soldiers, seamen, and aviators killed in ac tion who have never returned to New Zealand
and whose bodies are left, many of them, in unmarked graves on foreign shores.
Like many of us, she was driven by a deep  understanding of the strength of feeling
New Zealand has towards the sacrifice that  young men and women made to ensure our
freedom, democracy, and human rights, and al so by personal family experiences—from
uncles, great-uncles, fathers, and so on who had fought in the First World War and
Second World War.
I have to say that my regard for our old se rvicemen came from a very early age with
the emphasis that my parents put on honouring those who had served in those wars. In
June 2007 I represented the New Zealand Government at the 90th commemoration of the
Battle of Messines in Belgium, where 128 officers and soldiers are buried at the
Messines Ridge cemetery, thousands of kilome tres from home. They died defending
people they did not know. It was the battle where Lance Co rporal Samuel Frickleton, a
South Island coal miner, won his Victoria Cross. I was moved by the gratitude still felt
by the people in that tiny village of Messines—a village twinned with Featherston in
New Zealand. In the museum that you will find in that village, I found the names of two
young men killed in action from my home town of Murchison. When you consider what
a tiny town that is and that two men had lost  their lives in that battle, that certainly
moved me.
On 24 April 2007 Helen Clark and I announced  plans for a New Zealand memorial
park at the National War Memorial precinct, and $10.9 million of funding was allocated
at that point. Wellington City Council also committed funding. We worked closely with
the former mayor Kerry Prendergast on this  matter. It was the accumulation of several
years of work. From the time of the return  of the Unknown Warrior, work was started
on the idea of a National War Memorial Park. It started by ensuring that we were able to
acquire the land. Because the land actually wa s zoned semi-industrial, we needed to be
able to acquire that land for the park to  proceed. We worked w ith the Wellington City
Council on that proposal.
I was disappointed when I heard on the radio at the time this bill was announced
criticism from the Green Party about the dela y by Labour for this park. In fact, it was
quite wrong. A lot of work had been done from the time that the Unknown Warrior was
brought home to the time we went out of Go vernment. You had to finish the inner-city
bypass to ensure that you were able to pres erve that land for a park. We also worked
with the Wellington City Council, because at that time it wanted the continuation of a
tree-lined avenue up Taranaki Street that c ould then link in with the park. This is the
sort of work that was going on when we were in Government.
The key political point, if there is one to be made, is that it could have been done
without legislation if th e National Government had not mucked around with the
proposal for the last 4 years. Chris Finlayson, who has just introduced the bill, made it
very clear to the Wellington C ity Council just afte r the 2008 election that he was not
going to continue with Helen Clark’s vision. I am pleased that he now talks of caring for
the children and so on, but he did not wish to continue with her vision. It always seemed
to me to be rather petty, because this was a vision, as he said, that we should embrace
for all New Zealanders.
So putting aside the petty politics that have been played with the memorial park, we
do want to see a National War Memorial Park  that the nation will be proud of at the
100th anniversary of Gallipoli in 1915. It is a park openi ng that I would be very
honoured to attend and, hopefully, will be attending as the sixth Labour Government.
The passing of this empowering legisla tion should not be done lightly. This is
empowering legislation, and we always need to  be careful when we give such power to
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4807
this Parliament, but there is strong support from the local community, from the
Wellington City Council, and from our vete ran organisations. So with the strong
support and with the desire to have it finished by 2015, and the need to make sure that it
will be finished, we will support this empowering legislation.
But there are some changes that we would like to see made at the select committee,
and I believe that the Minister of Transport,  at least, is entert aining these amendments
that we are putting up. We would like to se e the role of the re view panel that is
established in the legislation widened to in clude oversight of the consents that are
granted. Given the range of the consents an d the overriding of the appeal rights, we
think that that would give the public confiden ce in the process if the review panel had
this role. This is especially important in terms of environmental and heritage
considerations. Secondly, we would like to see the review panel report on its work on a
regular basis—6 monthly—to a select committe e such as, say, the Regulations Review
Committee. Thirdly, we would like to see prior consultation procedures with interested
stakeholders before Orders in Council ar e proposed. The community forum that has
been established in legislation could, we be lieve, fulfil this role. Fourthly, we would
also like to put into law a role for the comm unity forum in being consulted on the final
design of the park. Incidentally, the local  MP, Grant Robertson, does have some
concerns with elements of the design of the park, particularly around vehicle access, but
he has been working this through with members of the Government.
We support the undergrounding of Buckle Street , but we have to say that it is going
to be rather a funny roa d. We have now just had announced by the New Zealand
Transport Agency the flyover that is going to go round the Basin Reserve. This road is
now going to look like a roller-coaster road, where you go under, you go up, you go
down, you go up, and you head to the tunnel at Mount Victoria. I do say to the
Government that maybe Maurice Williamson can take this up, as he is probably the only
Minister here who has some knowledge of these things. When we underground the road
at Buckle Street, we might look at whether a flyover is actually appropriate, unless we
do really want a roller coaster. I have to sa y that it has been a ro ller-coaster ride for
those of us in Wellington looking to see wh at the Government was finally going to do
around the congestion in the city. We know now that  it is going to be this roller-coaster
ride up to the Mount Victoria tunnel. You will be able to get very fast to the Mount
Victoria tunnel, but then, of course, you will go through just a one-lane tunnel.
Although you will get there quickly, you will get through the tunnel more slowly.
We do say to the Government that this, in the wider sense, is a great idea—the park.
We will support it, but look at what you are doing with the other roads round the Basin
Reserve leading to Mount Victoria. We do not want it to look foolish when we finally
open it in 2015. The Labour Party will be supporting this bill, and we will be giving all
assistance and advice we can to the Govern ment to make sure it goes through in the
timetable that has been set.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: I rise on behalf of the ACT Party to support
the first reading of the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill. Of
course, as previous speakers have said, th e bill seeks to give the Government the
necessary statutory au thority to complete the memorial park by April 2015. This is a
timely bill in our history. It will be the 100-year anniversary of the Australian and New
Zealand Army Corps landing at Anzac C ove on the Gallipoli peninsula in the
Dardanelles on that fateful morning of 25 April 1915—lest we forget. The disastrous
Gallipoli campaign gave birth to the Anzac spirit of comradeship and bravery beyond
all odds. It contributed much to our sense of national identity. Th is empowering bill is
as much about national identity as it is about  an empowering bill that will enable us to
4808 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
put in place a long-living memorial to those brave souls who lost their lives in such
great numbers on that first day, and days thereafter 25 April 1915.
Today Anzac Day commemorates all our brave fallen from the Western Front and
other theatres of war—World Wa r II to the conflicts in Korea, Malaysia, and Viet Nam
to modern places of conflict in East Timo r and currently, much in our minds, to the
conflict in northern Afghanistan, where th e brave men and women of New Zealand
stand in harm’s way. In Anzac Day we still celebrate the close bonds of friendship and
family with our Australian cousins and our sh ared sacrifice at Gallipoli since then with
our Australian cousins. Some have said th at Anzac Day is as close as New Zealand has
to a national day. I would ag ree with that. In part th is results from our annual
controversy around Waitangi Day.
However, I believe the better explanation is that Anzac Day does not celebrate war as
the great adventure; rather, it reminds us of the tragedy and utter waste of war, the
longing for family and the familiar. We reme mber the young New Zealanders buried in
some corner of a foreign field. We l ook to our own families where most have
experienced loss and disabil ity from war, and those who have had family members in
the service of New Zealand. In short, An zac Day speaks directly to the shared
experiences of most extended New Zealand families more than any other day in our
national life. This is what this empowering bill is all about.
I am glad that this is a shared be lief and commitment from all corners of the
Parliament. As the number of active servic e personnel who experience conflict falls in
real terms, it is even more important that we remind ourselves annually of the horror
and loss of war, and reaffirm and confirm our commitment to the young men and
women who stand ready to go into armed conflict on our behalf on any day. So this bill
will enable the building of a memorial park. As a Wellingtonian born and bred, that is a
very fitting place of national commemorati on and national mourni ng—the capital city
of the country.
All New Zealanders should be proud of this day and what this empowering bill
follows and what this piece of legislation will  deliver. It does so by granting the right to
the New Zealand Transport Agency and the Chief Executive of the Ministry for Culture
and Heritage to design, construct, maintain, and operate the park during the construction
and alteration of this significant piece of our roading network. It requires mitigation of
an actual or potential adverse environmental e ffect. It provides a series of statutory
powers that are incidental to this objective.  The extensive schedules to the bill, which
run to a mind-numbing 92 pages, essentiall y provide what would be in a resource
consent issued by the Wellington Regional Council and the Wellington City Council. In
essence, the project is to cut and cover Bu ckle Street to deve lop a contiguous park
directly linked to the Hall of Memories a nd the Tomb of the Unknown Warrior. I salute
all of those who have been re sponsible for the design of th is everlasting memorial, and
the complexities of what they have been gi ven and what they have  had to work with.
This, of course, will provide appropriate space for ceremonies involving our service
personnel and a place for memorials for those nations that are closest to us.
I acknowledge the work of Ministers Finlay son and Brownlee, fo r their persistence
and tenacity, and delivering this today at this  time for this memorial. I also place on
record the contribution of the Wellington City Council and, in particular, the
outstanding individual Ian McKinnon, th e Deputy Mayor of the Wellington City
Council. We hope that the memorial park w ill be a place where Ne w Zealanders will
visit to reflect and remember our fallen. This is a bipartisan memorial, and I salute all of
those former Prime Ministers, arts and cult ure Ministers, and me mbers of Parliament
from the Wellington district who have co mmitted to this memorial, and who will vote
for this today through their affiliations in this Parliament.
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4809
So it is with some caution that I want to make this observation to the House in
passing. I accept fully the Government’s cont ention that this worthy project cannot be
completed in 18 months. In most other developed countries it could easily be completed
within 18 months within a standard cons enting process. This speaks not to the
complexity of this worthy project but rath er to the unwieldy effect of the Resource
Management Act 1991. I sat in this Parliament, opposite on the front bench of this
Parliament, and then on the Government side  of the Parliament in 1991, where at 11
o’clock at night in a third reading 7-minute dissertation by the Minister of the time the
Resource Management Act was posted unani mously on to the statute book by this
Parliament, with little understanding of the consequences that would follow the
implementation and interpretation of the Re source Management Act over 20 years. It
has been, in general terms, a complete disast er for growth, investment, and jobs for this
nation, and that is why the ACT Party is at the forefront of two tranches of reform to the
Resource Management Act, which is well overdue . If there is one flagpole that should
be attended to today and a flag raised, it is the flag for democracy, it is the flag for
private property ownership, and it is the flag  for development, grow th, and jobs that is
well overdue here.
We should not replicate the Resource Mana gement Act high jinks that cost the
constituent ratepayers of the Auckland C ity Council $10 million in cost overruns in
building the refurbished, redeveloped art ga llery in Auckland City—that is $10 million
of political high jinks around the Resource Management Act and the Environment Court
by a litigious handful of people, which cost us so much money. It is entirely appropriate
that we continue to expand and perfect our freedoms so that those who were sent and
did not return from places that are list ed on the battlefield plaques around this
Parliament are not disappointed in this new century around an Act of Parliament that
stops sensible stuff like this happening. New Zealand, after 100 years have passed,
remains committed to the memory of those br ave souls who fought the battles recorded
on the walls around this Chamber, and soon to be recorded with a new memorial for the
100-year commemoration of that fateful day of 25 April 1915.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.
I wonder whether you could give the member who has just resumed his seat, the Hon
John Banks, the opportunity to correct his Hansard, in that it was not Labour that
passed the Resource Management Act—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is a debatable
issue, and the member is a very, very experienced one.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: After the speech from
that member, which strayed so far from the substance of this bill, can I say that it is
rather amusing to hear Mr Banks from the ACT Party speaking so passionately about a
memorial. It will be a memorial to that memb er and his party that will be constructed in
the not too distant future.
I do want to come back to a very impor tant piece of legislation. The Labour Party
will be supporting the National War Memo rial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill,
despite the truncated select committee proce ss, which requires the bill to be reported
back by 18 September, and despite the fact  that this bill overrides aspects of the
Resource Management Act. We are a constr uctive Opposition party and we do want to
work with the Government, where it is appropr iate, on a project that truly is of national
significance. It is a pleasure to finally see a roading project that is of genuine national
significance.
It completes, as other members have sa id, a memorial project that was first
envisioned, really, immediately after the Firs t World War, or the Great War, as it was
known at the time—a time when New Zealand was reeling from the deaths of over
4810 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
18,000 of our people who went to Europe and served on behalf of our nation and on
behalf of the British Empire. Countless othe rs were injured and countless families were
impacted by that really ast onishing conflict, at a time wh en the Industrial Revolution
had delivered the firepower to create untold damage to people, to buildings, and to the
landscape, but had not yet delivered the manoeuvrability for soldiers, sailors, and
airmen and women to be able to manoeuvre around that firepower.
The effects were devastating, and it was out of that devastation that Prime Minister
William Massey first explored the idea of a war memorial, which, of course, was first
constructed in 1932, with the Carillon, followe d a few decades later with the Hall of
Memories, then early this century with the Tomb of the Unknown Warrior, and now this
project to complete the memorial, which is, obviously, not just to those people who
served in the Great War, the First World Wa r, but also, ultimately, to those who served
in South Africa, in the Second World War, in Korea, in Malaysia, and in Viet Nam. Of
course, we will soon need to add to that li st the veterans of our peacekeeping activities
in East Timor and those in the Solomon Islands, where we have been lucky enough not
to lose anybody in combat, a nd, of course, what is really  front of mind for all New
Zealanders at the moment, those who have fallen in the conflict in Afghanistan. Of
course, we particularly remember the five who have fallen this month.
They will be remembered in this National War Memorial Park. It will be a place
where New Zealanders can pause, reflect on that sacrifice made over the generations by
New Zealanders, reflect on what it means to build a peaceful world, what it means to
live in a peaceful nation, and what it mean s to create tolerance and understanding, and
reflect on our work to find a future without conflict and without that level of sacrifice. It
is for all those reasons that we do support this piece of legislation.
It is disappointing, though—and I am sure th ere will be a lot of people out there who
will be disappointed—that it requires this em powering legislation that does override the
Resource Management Act, and that real traction on this project has taken such a
tremendously long time. The idea of the memori al park was first ar ticulated by the then
Prime Minister, Helen Clark, at the time that the Tomb of the Unknown Warrior was
first unveiled. Progress was made through to  2008. As recently—well, as long ago, in
fact—as 2009, the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage, Chris Finlayson, was saying
in response to questions from his own b ackbenchers that the Government had the
project in hand, that it did not necessarily want to carry on  with the vision that Helen
Clark had articulated, but that it was making good progress. We ll, it is lamentable that
the progress was not as solid as was made out  by the Minister at th at time and we find
ourselves now, more than 3 years after that event, debating a bill that gives the
Government the ability to rush a project that did not need to be rushed.
But, as I have said, we in the Labour Party wish to be constructive, and we know that
this is a project that New Zealanders want to see fulfilled, and that we now need to put
aside the unfortunate delay and get on with the project. However, we also need to
acknowledge that this legislation gives the Government significant power, and we need
to have the right checks and balances in place to ensure that that power is used
appropriately and wisely.
We are committed to the memorial park and we support this legislation, but we do
want to see some changes, and we hope  that these changes are given proper
consideration, despite the truncated select committee process. The role of the review
panel that is established in the legislati on needs to be widened, in our opinion, to
include oversight of the consents that are granted. Given the range of consents and the
overriding of appeal rights, we think that it would be right and would give public
confidence to the review proce ss if the review panel had th is role. It is especially
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4811
important in terms of the environment and heritage considerations that will go along
with this project.
The review panel needs to be able to report on its work regularly. We think that a 6-
monthly basis would be appropr iate. We think that report should be made to a select
committee, and the most appropriate appears to be the Regulations Review Committee.
We would also like to see pr ior consultation procedures w ith interested stakeholders
before Orders in Council are proposed. The co mmunity forum that is established in this
legislation could easily fulfil this role. Fina lly, we would also like to see put into the
legislation a role for the community forum in  being consulted on the final design of the
park. We think this is just simply about ensu ring that what is crea ted is something that
the community can appreciate, and that they will be able to buy into.
As I said, this is the completion of a vi sion that truly goes all the way back over
nearly the full century that the completion of this memorial pa rk will acknowledge on
25 April 2015. It is the completion of a vision that many Prime Ministers have
articulated, most recently, of course, Helen Clark, who was so instrumental in ensuring
that that Unknown Warrior was brought back to New Zealand, and that we had that
focal point of our memorials. This memorial  park will be a prope r completion of this
project, and something for all New Zealanders  to celebrate—truly a project of national
significance.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Just before I call the next
member, can I just advise members about the use of electronic devices. When not being

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia
ora. I rise to take a cal l on the National War Memorial  Park (Pukeahu) Empowering
Bill. The Green Party supports the National War Memorial Park, but we will not be
supporting the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill at its first
reading. We support the memorial. We support a park. As a Wellingtonian, I am excited
by the idea that we will get a bit of green sp ace, a bit of quiet space, in an otherwise
pretty busy and hectic part of the town in Mount Cook. We think it is important that we
do commemorate the people who have falle n and are immortalised around this
Chamber. I was recently in London, where I got to see the new New Zealand war
memorial in downtown London. It is a great example, I feel, of how we can have
modern war commemorations that do not use the traditional mould. I note that Australia
has still got the traditional one in the park, next to ours. They can be powerful emotional
reflections of our national character, and I think that it is a good example of that.
The Green Party will not be supporting the bill, because it is drafted in such a manner
that overrides the Resource Management Act,  the Historic Places Act, and the Public
Works Act, and takes from the Canterbur y Earthquake Recovery Act the provisions
whereby further rules can be amended by Orde rs in Council. I think it is important to
reflect on why the Green Party is opposed to this bill. We are opposed to this because it
is a damaging precedent in our democracy. I have gone through the history. I am aware
of a number of bills and Acts that have been enacted by this Parliament over the years to
enact transport projects like the Tauranga expressway, and there are a few more, like the
Auckland Harbour Bridge, but none of them used the powers—the immense and
considerable powers—outlined in  this bill to override legi slation. In fact, the only
examples that the Parliamentary Library c ould find this afternoon were the Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery Act and the Rugby Wo rld Cup 2011 (Empowering) Act, which
were passed in this current Government’s time on the Government benches. This is the
only Government that is drafting laws that allow itself to override any laws—or, in this
4812 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
case, a constrained number of laws—that it wants to override. This is the only
Government that is drafting laws that allo w it to amend future laws through Orders in
Council. We think it is a damaging, dangerous precedent. Although we do not think it is
likely to be abused under this law, we do not th ink it is the path this Parliament or this
country should be going down. We support the democratic rights of law, the due
process, that our soldiers went overseas to serve and to protect.
I have not heard from the Government or  from the Labour Part y benches the reason
why we have to have legisla tion to override these three laws and to give themselves
other powers through Order in Council. What is the reason? I think we all know, but it
is embarrassing because we do not want to me ntion it, and that is that the Government
has not given itself enough time to enact it, to get the time to go through the normal
processes, because the Government scrapped it. The history is that in 2004 Helen Clark
first announced the formation of this par k, which the Green Party supported. In 2007
Labour put $10 million towards it. In 2009 it wa s the Government, in its line by line
review, that removed the funding. The only re ason why we have to do this, I think,
amazing and dangerous precedent step of passing laws to build a road and a park is that
the Government has not given itself e nough time to do it, because the Government
scrapped the money. The Government has raided  the transport pantry and there is not
enough money left for projects like this becau se the Government would rather spend it
on seven uneconomical roads of national signif icance. This is the real issue we should
be addressing. Although I would like to stre ss that the Green Party supports the war
memorial and we support the park, we do not support the process that is going through.
We are seeing the same pattern emerge when it comes to the select committee
consideration—a constrained time for New Z ealanders, for Wellingtonians, to have a
say.
What we are concerned about, of course, is  we are going to get a less than ideal
process. The point of having an open a nd appropriate length of time for public
consultation and processes through the Re source Management Act or the Historic
Places Act is so we make the right decisions. What we are concerned about is we are not
going to see the right decisi ons being made. We are not  going to see maybe common-
sense decisions to mitigate an unfortunate side effect or impact of this project, because
the Government wants to race it through becau se it has run out of time, because the
Government is a poor manager. That is the real reason why we ha ve to go through this
unprecedented step.
The Green Party wants to see it done right. We want to see proper processes, and that
is why we will not be supporting this bill. We will go into the Transport and Industrial
Relations Committee with a constructive manner. We would like to improve this bill,
but it has to be pointed out that, look, this road is only 5 years old and this Government,
at a time of austerity, at a time of debt crisis, has all this mo ney to dig up a road that is
only 5 years old and it has to  do it through legislation be cause of its bad decision-
making. It is a shocking state of affairs, and that is why I am proud to be a member of
the party that is voting against it today.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to
speak in regard to the National War Memori al Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill. First
of all, I would like to thank the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage for his
introduction to this bill. I would like to ma ke special mention of the Labour Party and
thank its members for the way they have spoken on this bill and for the work that they
have done in the past, and also for the agre ement from them to help in the select
committee stage as we go through this somewh at truncated process. I would like to
draw special attention to the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee members
from the Labour Party, who are very helpful and can work well w ith all parties to
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4813
achieve the right things for this country. I think it is important for us to note that this is a
bipartisan approach.
It is very disappointing, however, to hear  from the Green Party, which has now left
the Chamber, that it does not support this bill.

items.speaker: Holly Walker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speake r. I believe it is inappropriate for
the member to refer to the absence of another member from the Chamber.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Actually, the member is
right. If he did do that, then he should not . But I never heard him say that. The member
is saying he did not do it?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I said the Green Party, not the member.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I think the member did
breach the convention, but, just for Holly Wa lker, it is a convention, rather than a

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Can I just say that members
should look at Speaker’s ruli ng 24/4. It is inappropriate to refer to the absence of
