items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: But I think it is sad that the Green Party will not support this
bill. When it talks about the Resource Management Act and a road being 5 years old,
and that in times of austerity you do not want  to take the road up and do anything, that
is just rubbish, to be honest. This is some thing that many Parliaments have worked on
over many years. It is something that is in the best interests of us as a country to think of
the culture and heritage of our country. It is about paying tribute to those people who
have made sacrifices for the freedoms we en joy here in this room today. It is about
having some pride in our history and doing th e right thing. Maybe this will be a lesson
for the Green Party, should it ever be close to getting into Government, that it may need
to do the right thing when it is in Government  and not what it thinks necessarily is in its
best interests.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: If, David.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: That is a big if, as the Minister says. It is very sad that in this
House those members have not agreed to this  bill today. But they did ask one question,
and that is why you want to do it. There is a reason, and that is to  get it finished by
2015, and that is what this bill is enabling the Government to do. It is to make sure that
the effort that has gone in in past years is completed, so that we have it ready in time for
April 2015. That is a very im portant date on our  political calendar  and also on our
country’s calendar.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Annette could be mayor when it’s opened.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Yes, we may have Annette as mayor when it opens, we are
hearing. This bill grants the necessary authorisations and property rights and works with
the different departments to achieve this purpose. We look forward to Annette being
there as the mayor. That should be an interes ting process, if that comes to fruition as
well.
This bill represents an important part of  our culture and our history. The symbolism
of memorial parks is very  valid and important. Wellingt on is the capital of New
Zealand. It is a place where you have large ar t and cultural meaning for this country. It
is a place where Parliament is based. It is also fitting that we have a memorial of this
stature and calibre to represen t the immense sacrifices and the pride that we take in our
country’s past and also in our ability to go forward together. I would like to recommend
this bill to the House. I would like to tha nk the Minister and also the Labour Party for
4814 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
their support. We look forward to other part ies in this House supporting it as it goes
through. Thank you.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First on
the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill. New Zealand First will
be, of course, supporting this bill and supporti ng this initiative of the Government and
the other agencies, including Wellington Ci ty Council, the New Zealand Transport
Agency, and the Ministry for Culture and Her itage. We believe this  is a very worthy
project as we approach the centenary of World War I, and it is very fitting that such a
project is undertaken as a significant milest one in the commemorations of some of our
most notable parts of New Zealand history.
For those of us who have been to th e National War Memorial on a number of
occasions, we are always most impressed with the memorial itself, the wonderful
building that is there, and what it offers in  terms of that building structure. But it has
always been my impression that it is a great shame that the road immediately in front of
it is a busy road. In a sense, you know, it is a big drawback from the war memorial that
is there and the National War Memorial building. It is not fitting that it is such a busy
arterial route. When you compare it with the great capitals of the world and their
national memorials, and you think of the likes of Canberra, and you think of the likes of
Washington DC—my youngest daughter, Bryony, was in Washington DC this week and
she commented on being able to walk around  and see the marvellous monuments and
the wonderful memorials in Washington DC—it is very notable that in many countries a
huge amount of national pride is often in th eir national war memori als. We have also
seen that in more recent years with the w onderful memorials that have been developed
in London, including the New Zealand memorial that is there now in Hyde Park. So I
think it is very fitting that finally New Zealand should ma ke its National War Memorial
an even more fitting place, something with a little bit more peace and tranquillity, and
something with a little bit more of the natu ral New Zealand quiet ambience, rather than
a busy road roaring straight past the memorial.
I have looked at the concept drawings a nd the concept designs for this, and it is a
beautiful park that is envisaged there, with the former road disappearing underneath and
well out of sight and sound. As a result, it will allow larger numbers of people to go and
visit the war memorial and ta ke in the whole ambience and feeling of the place. Also,
when there are parades—and I have been to  a number of parades there—it will be a
much nicer place for our veterans, for our m ilitary, for those involved with the parades,
and for the public who are attending to ha ve a more fitting, peaceful, and more
observant commemoration.
I was talking with my colleague Richard Pryor here before. Both of us have
attended—not Richard Pryor; Richard Prosser.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Prosser. Prosser.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: Sorry. It is not a day for surnames, is it, Mr Assistant
Speaker? I apologise to my co lleague, and I am sure he wi ll call me names afterwards,
as well.
But Richard Prosser and I were just noti ng that we have both attended Anzac Day
ceremonies at the Anzac War Memorial in th e centre of Sydney, and how lovely that is
with the ponds and the park that surrounds it, and how it is such a wonderful, fitting
situation for their Anzac Day ceremonies. I can see this being the same situation for the
capital city of our country. This park in the future will be a wonderful place for more
and more people to go to. Being an Aucklande r, I say that we are very proud of our
cenotaph up there in the mi ddle of the Auckland Domain, next to the Auckland War
Memorial Museum, and how wonderful it is  to have that surrounded by such a large
expanse of green space. Similarly, it would be very appropriate for the capital city to
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4815
have a similar park of a reasonable size around the National War Memorial, so that,
again, it can be commemorated in that way.
We owe a great debt to our veterans, and as the veterans’ affairs spokesman for New
Zealand First, I say that we are very conscious of honouring them and remembering
them. Here in this Chamber, when we look at the names around the walls here, there are
great names such as Passchendaele behind me, Gallipoli over there, Messines, and
Egypt. There are so many wonderful names, a nd of course more recent ones such as
Viet Nam, Korea, Malaya, and others. Wh ile we honour our veterans and our great
commitment to keeping world peace around the world, it is very fitting that we also do
this at our National War Memorial in this way.
Much of the cost does involve the actual road, and many people who perhaps are not
so enthusiastic about this might look at the cost, but much of that is taken up in the
actual tunnelling of this road, which is going to be of long-term benefit to Wellington
and long-term benefit to traffic movements in  that area. Effectively, the park costs and
the memorial costs are an insignificant amount in the greater scheme of things.
We believe that this legislation is important. Time is of the essence. It will take a
reasonable amount of time to get this proj ect completed. We cannot  wait until after the
World War I commemorations to have it completed, so it is important that it is done in a
timely fashion. In matters of national impor tance such as this, where we would hope
there would be agreement across the House to get this done, we would certainly look to
have this bill expedited through this House as quickly as possible so that this project can
really get some traction and really make some progress very, very quickly.
Just in closing, New Zealand First supports this. We think it is very, very timely. It is
another way that we can honour those who have  fallen in the name of our country, and
who have made the ultimate sacrifice for this country. They have made the ultimate
sacrifice on behalf of our nation, in order fo r us to be the good democracy that we are.
In that respect this is a very, very small price to pay to ensure that we continue to
honour what is a great legacy that has been left  by those who have fallen in the past and
by those who have gone off to war on behalf of New Zealand. So Ne w Zealand First is
very happy to commend this bill to the House, and we will be supporting it.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: It is a genuine pleasure to speak in favour
of this piece of legislation, the Nationa l War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering
Bill, and it has been very good to see, you know, the working together of the parties,
with the exception of one, on this bill, and the genuine and the passionate and the well-
intentioned speeches of all members so far on this piece of legislation.
I was listening very carefully to the speech  of the Minister for Arts, Culture and
Heritage. It was good to hear that when the war memorial was first established in this
country, it was a unanimous vote in this Parlia ment that saw it established. As we come
close to the centenary of the Gallipoli landings and as we ta lk about a project that is
designed to commemorate not only that landi ng and that war but also other conflicts
that New Zealanders have served this country well in in overseas theatres, remembering
those people and commemorating the sacrifice that they have made for this country, it is
fitting that we should also have cross-party support in this Chamber.
I would ask those who have indicated some opposition to this bill to really reconsider
whether or not that is the right thing to be doing. Yes, there are some questions about
the process. Yes, there are some people w ho may have some unease at the fact that
legislation of this type is being proposed or is going through this Parliament in the
fashion that it is, but we have to remember the importance and the significance of this
project. We have to remember that we want  to see this project in place and completed
by Anzac Day in 2015, and to fail to meet that deadline would be absolutely
unacceptable.
4816 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
I listened carefully also to the speech fr om the Hon Annette King, and I was pleased
to hear of all the work that Labour did for the National War Memorial. The Minister for
Arts, Culture and Heritage, Chris Finlays on, also spoke at great length about the
consultation and the efforts that he has put in as Minister, on behalf of this Government,
to try to get the National War Memorial to the point where we can have the park to
remember New Zealanders in 2015.
Looking through the regulatory impact statem ent there are some interesting points
that are worth noting, and I would like to co ver just a couple of those. I was quite
interested to see that there was some rece nt consultation done w ith the community in
2011. It was around the Wellington Northern Co rridor road of national significance.
There were many hundreds of submissions to that process, and 550 of those
submissions indicated that they would like to see a realignm ent or a redesign of Buckle
Street. So this legislation and the proposal we have in front of us would fulfil the wishes
of those 550 submitters.
It was also interesting to see in the regulat ory impact statement that a lot of work has
gone in with the Wellington City Council, th e New Zealand RSA, and indeed Mt Cook
School, all of which have indicated their support for this option. There is support from a
very wide range of people for this particular pr oject, and it is important that those
people’s wishes, as well as the wishes of a ll New Zealanders to have a grand memorial
for the centenary of the Gallipoli landings, is in place in time.
In terms of the process, yes, there is some legislation that is being proposed here that
would override some normal processes that we would go through, but I think it is
important to note in the House that there ar e also some important safeguards that are
being put into this le gislation. Firstly, there is the disa llowance procedure that is in the
legislation. When such wide-ranging powers w ould be granted to the Governor-General
to make Orders in Council, it is appropriate  that the disallowance  procedure be put in
place, and this bill does that.
This bill also establishes a community fo rum for ongoing consultati on with locals in
the area and interested stakeholders. Ther e is also a review panel that is being
established. Although it is not desirable in  the normal course of business to be
overriding other pieces of legisl ation in the fashion that this  does, for such a significant
project it is absolutely appropr iate, and the timing issue is essential so that we meet the
deadlines, the strict deadlines, we have for this project. The corresponding actions that
have been taken in the legislation ar ound review and around consultation are also
appropriate and should be welcomed, and th ey should mitigate many of the concerns
that some people may have.
This is a very, very important piece of le gislation to commemorate a very important
date when many thousands of New Zealande rs served their count ry in war, and I
commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: It is my pleasure to contribute to this
debate on the National War Memorial Pa rk (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill. This
legislation would not have b een necessary if National had not taken away the project
funding that Labour had allocated in the clos ing period of the fifth Labour Government.
The park would have been ready for the 2015 centenary of Gallipoli, and we would not
have had the need in this H ouse to pass empowering legisla tion if that had been done.
But I want to say that Labour supports this bill. We believe that New Zealanders will
see the need for this legislation and that New Zealanders will appreciate the plan that is
in place for this war memorial park.
I want to say to the Green Party members here today “Enough with the sanctimony.
Enough.” I feel absolute exasperation that the Greens would come here and lecture the
House on this bill because it overrides th e Resource Management Act, because it
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4817
overrides the Historic Places Act, and because  it overrides the Public Works Act. These
bits of legislation are not some kind of re ligion. They are not our constitution. They are
legislation that we have there to govern the process of resource management and land
use. They are practical bits of information that are there for practical purposes. With this
project, we are not rebuilding the Clyde Dam, and we are not desecrating some national
landscape. What we are doing is converting a piece of urban citys cape into what will
undoubtedly be a fantastic national memorial  for the people of Wellington and the
people of this country, and I urge the Greens to reconsider their position on this.
This, as Iain Lees-Galloway said, will be a park of national significance. I want to
just talk in the minutes remaining about how  this is an exercise in constructing and
building a special place in Wellington for pe ople to come—a place of contemplation, a
place of reflection. I think it wi ll be a tremendous contribution to our national life as a
country. Like other members will have done, I have looked at the c oncept drawings for
the memorial park and I think they are appr opriate. They are grand,  and they will leave
as a legacy for this country a really special  place for people to come and reflect on our
history and on the sacrifice that generati ons of New Zealanders—men and women who
fought overseas, and particularly those who gave their lives—have made.
I just want to stress how valuable it is to create places like this. There are one or two
others in New Zealand that I can think of. The Waitangi Treaty grounds are another
place where the history is palpable when you ar e there. It is a place of reflection, where
you can contemplate this nation’s modern hi story. I think, as Andrew Williams said,
that the cenotaph at the Auckland War Memori al Museum is another similar place. In
another city that I am familiar with, in Washington, DC, where I lived for several years,
the Lincoln Memorial was perhaps my favour ite of all the Washi ngton memorials—an
amazing place where people would go day and night to remember the abolition of
slavery, the civil war, and, in  fact, the civil rights moveme nt. That particular place in
Washington, DC is a remarkable place to go to visit, to soak up the ambience, and to
reflect on the country’s history.
I also want to just note that it is interesting, I think, that in order to create this park of
national significance, it is necessary to remove the traffic from this place. It would be
unthinkable to build a war memorial park of  the kind of scale a nd the ambition and the
quality that we will want for this park without getting cars out of it by building a tunnel.
Increasingly in our cities, peopl e are recognising that it is ti me to reclaim the streets of
our cities from the car, because when you—as we have done for so many years—build
cities around the motorcar, it creates uncivil ised environments that are not fit for
pedestrians, are not fit for people to spend any time in, an d are certainly not fit for
places of reflection or contemplation. I think that we are seeing more and more in our
cities a pedestrianisation and a reclaiming of our streets from the cars.
The last point that I wanted to make is a bout the number of provisions that Labour is
requesting be inserted into the bill as a c ondition of our supportin g the legislation. We
ask the Transport and Industrial Relations Co mmittee to consider these matters. First,
that the role of the review panel that is es tablished under this legislation be widened to
include oversight of the cons ents. Given the range of cons ents and the overriding of
appeal rights under this bill, we think it w ould give the public some confidence in the
process if the review panel is given this wi dened role. That is es pecially important in
terms of the environmental and heritage consid erations. We also believe that the review
panel should report on its work on a re gular—perhaps 6-monthly—basis to a select
committee such as the Regulations Review Co mmittee. We would also like to see prior
consultation procedures with interested st akeholders before Orders in Council are
proposed. The community forum that this bill  would establish coul d fulfil that role.
Finally, we would also like to  put into the law a role for the community forum in being
4818 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
consulted on the design of the park. I know  that Grant Roberts on, who is the local
member of Parliament, has some concerns about elements of the design of the park,
particularly around vehicle access. We think it would be useful to involve the local
community and interested parties in the design of the park.
This bill sets the stage for what we believe will be a fantastic memorial for those who
have given their lives overs eas for our country. It will  create an outstanding public
space in Wellington for all New Zealanders, and particularly for the people of the
Mount Cook community. This is going to be  an extraordinary addition to their
community. I want to finally pay tribute to  the former Prime Minister Helen Clark,
whose vision it was, after the opening of the Tomb of the Unknown Warrior, to develop
the national memorial in this way. Helen Clark had that vision, she took the initial steps,
funding was put in place, and the process was se t in motion to build this memorial park.
Labour is pleased that the Government has fi nally come to its senses and brought this
bill to the House. Thank you.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I rise to speak in favour of the National War
Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill—

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: A very good bill.
CHRIS AUCHINVOLE  —sponsored by the Minister for Arts, Culture and
Heritage, Chris Finlayson. It is, indeed, as the Hon Nathan Guy says, a very good bill,
and it has received accolades from pretty much all sides of the House. There was—

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: That’s going a little far.

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: Charles Chauvel supports it.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, no, no, I do not remember Mr Chauvel hearing all
of the debate, but he will—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Oh, it was better without the microphone.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: God gives some people a good voice. Mr Chauvel will
remember the remarks made by the Hon Annette King, which were praiseworthy indeed
of the concept, the design, the proposal, and the need, in fact, to have a place of
reverence in our capital city, because, really, we do not have one at the moment.
This empowering bill grants the necessary  statutory authoris ations and property
rights for the project to the New Zealand Transport Agency and the Ministry for Culture
and Heritage to complete the roading and landscaping in time for the 2015 Anzac Day
commemorations—100 years. The bill is vi tal to the creation of a National War
Memorial Park for Wellington, providing th e certainty necessary for its completion by
April 2015, while ensuring the inte gration of the park and roading networks within the
wider Wellington City.
If I may, without any undue offence, suggest  that Mr Hughes from the Green Party
was just a little mean-spirited, I thought, in concentrating on the sacrosanct nature—

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: They hate roads, the Greens.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: —well, on the sacrosanct nature of process. I think this is
an occasion when process can be fitted in to meet the requirement, and I am sure that
that will be the case.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Sanctimonious.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: It was a little sanctimonious, I guess. New Zealanders
attach a special importance to our military history as well as to our environmental
processes and the reverence we  continue to have for th ose who made the ultimate
sacrifice in the defence of this nation and what it stands for. Indeed, in October I hope to
be in Passchendaele, paying due reverence to great-uncles who went into that particular
dreadful battle where New Zealand lost so ma ny. It will be a moment of reflection. I
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4819
think it will be great that we have the same opportunity for New Zealanders, and for
people from overseas, to engage in reverence in New Zealand. It will be a fitting place
for Kiwis and others to congreg ate on major occasions or to  reflect at any time on these
great sacrifices.
The project will ensure that Anzac Day commemorations in 2015 will take place in a
new open space, flanked on either side by landscaped areas with trees, seating,
cycleways, and walking paths.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Very appropriate.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: It is, indeed, appropriate a nd befitting for such a historic
moment in the history of both our nation a nd our allies across the Tasman Sea. Indeed,
the Australian Government has contributed A$5 million of its own for the development
of an Australian memorial, which will st and with pride opposite the National War
Memorial as a symbol of the bond and the shared history between our two nations.

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: That’s right—the Anzac spirit.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: That is the Anzac spirit. This memorial plan has been
crafted with great care and respect. And it was again just a tad unfortunate when
listening to the Hon Annette King, whom I have great re spect for as a long-serving
politician, to hear a little sting in the tail that perhaps we have been dilatory over the last
4 years in getting things done . May I suggest, with great respect to Annette King, who
did leave Government with a plan, that that  plan was not simply dispensed with and
ignored. It was considered. There is a lot of  difference between being a little casual in
getting on with things and working extremely hard  to ensure the best results, and that is
what Mr Finlayson demanded from the team that has been working on this.
The memorial plan has been crafted with  great care and respect , but a number of
problems presently hinder the completion of this project by April 2015. These are
practical, physical problems, such as the busy State Highway 1, which is currently in the
way of the site and which is clearly incompa tible with a memorial status as a place of
quiet contemplation and reflection for fam ilies, dignitaries, and visitors. You cannot
have it quiet except for the cars. It is qui et or it is not. Also, under existing statutory
processes, it would be impossi ble to guarantee the necessary  statutory authorisations,
rights, and consents to see this project co mpleted on time, hence my mild criticism of
the Greens. The whole purpose of this bill is  to make sure that the project is done on
time. As my colleagues on this side have articulated, it is time to resolve these problems
once and for all.
Under this bill, the Governor-General will  be able to grant additional statutory
authorisations by Order in Council, and enable the relevant agencies to obtain additional
property rights in the event that any unfor eseen authorisation and rights are legally
required in order to complete the project on time, and to avoid, remedy, or mitigate any
actual or potential adverse effects on th e environment. We are not ignoring the
environment. Indeed, I think Annette Ki ng—whose speech I quite enjoyed, and I am
showing her that I listened—illustrated that you would have a tunnel underneath, a
flyover round the cricket grounds, and then go straight into the tunnel, like Hobbiton.
The bill also sets the conditions that will apply to the statutory authorisations, and
provides a process for the independent certifi cation of plans and documents required by
conditions of the authorisations. This is to ensure that both the New Zealand Transport
Agency and the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage comply with the usual
construction requirements and environmental standards that they would have had to
meet if the authorisations had been gr anted under normal process. The provisions
relating to Orders in Council and the remova l of appeal and object ion rights will expire
at the close of 31 July 2015.
4820 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
To put it simply, without this bill the de velopment of this site and its monuments
would not be possible on a timetable basis in the foreseeable future. This is a roll-your-
sleeves-up, grunty little bill that gets the job done. Underneath  that, or overarching that,
it will produce not only something that is prac tical and well done but something that is
beautiful, that we can all celebrate in, and that we can all enjoy. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Charles Chauvel, is this a split call?

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: It is, Mr Deputy Speaker. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you. Charles Chauvel. [Interruption]

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Well, here we go: a spiteful comment from the
Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage, setting the tone for the debate, as he has done in
respect of this matter ever since it began. The reality of this entire issue is that had that
member not held such a spiteful hatred for Helen Clark, which he repeats ad nauseam at
every opportunity, this legi slation, the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu)
Empowering Bill, would not be necessary. We would not be taking up Parliament’s
time with it at the moment, becau se the reality is that when Labour left office this park
was ready to go.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: No, it wasn’t.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Everything was ready—everything was ready—and that
member, because of his petty, spiteful, nasty, bitchy little hatred of Helen Clark, could
not stand the idea that this project would pr oceed as planned. So what did he do? Never
mind our proud traditions of bipartisansh ip around commemorating our fallen, and
never mind the need to expedite the comm emoration of Gallipoli; that member stopped
the project in its tracks.
That is why we are here tonight having to pass special legislation in its first
reading—legislation that on its face is objectionable because it suspends the Resource
Management Act and it suspends the planning  process. It is now a matter where Grant
Robertson and Annette King have had to go to Gerry Brownlee—not to that worthless
Minister Chris Finlayson, because that Minist er would not have any power or authority
to grant these guarantees—and Gerry Brownl ee, very properly, in the spirit of
bipartisanship, has said: “Yes. This isn’t an ideal situation. We will grant you some
concessions around process to make sure that  our suspension of the ordinary rules”—
our suspension of the ordinary rules, for ced on us by the spiteful Minister for Arts,
Culture and Heritage, who just cannot stand the idea of Helen Clark having credit for
anything—“actually proceeds.”
That is the position we are in tonight. Th e position that we on this side of the House
are in is that we are having to support this  legislation, because we are patriots. We do
want to see this park completed in good order and in time for the Gallipoli
commemorations. We do not like the fact that it has to be forced through this House
without Resource Management Act approvals , without the ordinary processes that
would normally apply to it, and that would have applied had the Minister sponsoring
this bill not allowed his spite to interfere with his judgmen t—his hatred of the idea of
Helen Clark having a legacy—and introduced this legislation, as he has done years late,
in order to expedite this project. That is the problem that we face tonight.
Contrary to what the earlier  speaker said, we are hard ly giving this legislation
accolades. We are saying, well, we are where we  are. The anniversary is important, it is
a couple of years away. This job should ha ve been completed by now, but, because of
the incompetence of the Minister, we are where we are and we are having to
contemplate special empowering legislation in  the great Muldoonist traditions of the
National Party in order to get this legislation through. That is the political reality.
Let me talk about the concessions that our deputy leader and our former deputy
leader have negotiated, as I unde rstand it, with the Minister of  Transport. First of all,
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4821
there is going to be a review panel. That will be established in the legislation and its role
will be widened to include oversight of the consents that are granted. Given the range of
the consents and the overriding of the appeal rights that would normally exist, we think
it will give some measure of public confiden ce to the process if the review panel has
this role. The review panel will report on a regular basis to a select committee—perhaps
the Regulations Review Committee or anot her committee—so that there is proper
parliamentary oversight. And there will be prio r consultation procedures with interested
stakeholders before Orders in Council are proposed. We also would like to see a role in
law for the community forum, which is propose d, so that it is required to be consulted
on the final design of the park.
This is not an ideal situation. We will be proud to see the memorial erected. It should
have been in place by now, and it would be ha d the events that I have described not
transpired. But, as I say, we are where we ar e. With the guarantees as to process that
Labour has negotiated, we will be supporting th is legislation to select committee, and
we hope that those guarantees will survive.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I am pleased to speak on be half of the Green Party on
this National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill. I want to start by
reiterating the Green Party’s,  and, indeed, I am sure, all members’, profound sorrow at
the loss of five of our soldiers  in Afghanistan in recent weeks.  This tragic loss, I think,
really throws the issue of how best to commemorate and how best to memorialise war
and our soldiers lost in armed conflict into a sharp and very tragic relief at this particular
time.
In that context I, first, wa nt to emphasise that the Green Party is fully in support of
having a National War Memorial Park. I thi nk that other members have commented on
the renewed interest in recent years in the commemoration of our military history, and,
in particular, the increased interest fr om young people in Anzac Day celebrations. We
support the creation of this park to allow greater space for that reflection and that
commemoration to take place, particularly to reflect on that tragic loss of life, both
historically and more recently; to consid er and question the ro le of war and armed
conflict; and to think about how best to promote peace. National war memorials, like
the park proposed in this bill, can help us to  do that and to do that  thinking as a nation,
and that is very important.
It is important to do this in time to mark the centenary of Gallipoli in 2015, which is,
clearly, a very significant anniversary. It al so has the benefit of creating some vital
public space in our capital c ity and for our national enjoyment. However, we cannot,
and do not, support the extraordinary powers sought by the Government in this bill—the
power to grant rights and consents by Orde r in Council without recourse to Parliament
and the power to override the Resource Management Act, the Historic Places Act, and
the Public Works Work—and the truncated se lect committee process that has been
proposed for this bill. There is an absurdly  short period of 3 weeks for the committee to
report back to the House.
I heard an earlier speaker—David Bennett, I believe it was—refer to the sacrifice
that has been made by our soldiers over hi story for the rights and freedoms that we
enjoy here in this House today. I say to the House that one of those rights and freedoms
is democracy and responsible Government. We do not honour those rights and freedoms
that our soldiers fought for by brushing the la w aside in order to build a war memorial,
which could have been done in a timely fa shion had it not been prevaricated on and
cancelled by the current Government. It c ould have been built on time, with due
process, and probably less cost if the G overnment had not can celled funding for the
project in 2009. The reason we are here today,  looking at this extraordinary legislation
in an extraordinarily short time frame, is th at prevarication. There would have been no
4822 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012
need for this legislation, as the previous speaker has pointed out, and the bill could have
proceeded with the cross-party support that it deserves.
What this bill does is continue a pattern of behaviour from this Government in giving
itself extraordinary powers to override the law wh en it is inconvenient. We have seen it
with the dismissal of the Environment Canter bury councillors, we have seen it with the
creation of Orders in Counc il in relation to the Canter bury Earthquake Recovery
Authority in Christchurch, and we have seen it with the Auckland super-city. This bill is
just another example of this Government pushing the law to one  side when it is deemed
politically convenient to do so.
I want to address some of the comments made by Phil Tw yford, an earlier speaker,
because I was actually quite surprised to hear from him some pretty dismissive
comments about due process. He said that the Resource Management Act is just a piece
of paper. He said that it is not our constitution; it is just a piece of pa per. He said that it
is not like we are ramming through some out standing landscape. That is what Phil
Twyford said. I wonder whether Charles Chau vel heard that speech, because I agree
with Charles Chauvel in his previous contribut ion, just now, that elements of this bill
are very objectionable from a process perspect ive. If the Labour Party really does think
that we can put them to one side in such an easy manner, then I find that quite
concerning.
The Green Party will look to engage construc tively and to improve this bill in the
select committee. I am pleased to hear from Labour members some of the likely
concessions that they have negotiated. Those are the kinds of things that may make it
more palatable. Our support at this stage is  open. We are voting against this bill at its
first reading at the moment only, because we have such profound concerns with the
process. Thank you.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): “At the going down of the sun and in
the morning We will remember them.” I think that is the context in which we debate
this National War Memorial Park (Pukea hu) Empowering Bill. Although I will turn
some attention to the comments from the O pposition, I think it is important to remind a
previous speaker, Mr Chauvel, that—not th at I am a military ma n myself—a frontal
attack on to an entrenched position using words like “spiteful” and “hate” is actually
fraught with danger, and you will get shot to pieces, if not by me necessarily.
This is an incredibly important bill. Ev ery bill that comes before this House is
important, and every bill by its nature is democratic, as it is debated and discussed. As I
begin, I do want to take umbrage with the previous speaker, Holly Walker, and others
from the Green Party, in particular, who ha ve talked about this bill as being anti-
democratic and not following process and so forth. I sort of think, ipso facto, the fact
that we are standing here in this House, progressing a piece of legislation through its
stages, debating and discussing, is, by its nature, democratic.
But, you see, the Greens betrayed themselv es when they made an earlier comment
that “We are willing to work  with anyone.” Yes, they are—so long as everyone agrees
with them. I might need to remind the Greens that that is not democracy. Democracy is
about difference and debate and coming to a c onsensus. It is, if I may use the words of
Phil Twyford, sanctimonious to stand and lecture people that consensus means
accepting only a particular viewpoint. I think it is also most unfortunate that people like
me and others have had to react tonight to  this debate, in what has been a really
important discussion on a war memorial to honour our war dead.
I think it is important, too, to acknowledge what generally has been a very positive
debate. I do want to acknow ledge previous speakers, in cluding from the Greens, who
have uttered some very positive words, but particularly speak ers from Labour, from
New Zealand First—even if they might ge t their colleague’s name wrong occasionally,
28 Aug 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 4823
and I myself will probably fall into that tr ap now. There were some really positive
statements here.
It is important that we remember. Reme mbrance is an importa nt element of our
human nature, an important part, because to remember is an attempt to not repeat the
mistakes. We stand in a House of memory here. Different speakers have talked about
the plaques that are on the wall and have ac knowledged, too, the tragedies of the five
deaths in recent weeks. Memory  of these events is important. So, as we turn now to the
National War Memorial, the Carillon, and the development of the park, it is important
that we can create a space that enables us as Kiwis, as we approach 100 years since
1915, to remember. But remembering is not just an action of the past but an action now,
of the current. We have men and women serving overseas—fine men and women with
families—who are there serving us and continuing  to serve. So it is really important, as
we debate this bill, and as we remember in 2015, when this national park is opened, that
we acknowledge not only those who have served  us in the past but those who continue
to serve us now.
There has been some discussion that there is not enough due process. I think it is
important quickly to turn to the first words of the Minister for Arts, Culture and
Heritage, about the array of discussions that have been had—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Over 4 years.
SIMON O’CONNOR : Over 4 years, the Minister  reminds me; over 4 years of
discussions with parties across the country, he re in Wellington. It is vitally important to
put that in context, because th is bill is not an affront to the Resource Management Act.
This is not an affront to previous legislat ion. This is an opportunity to take those
discussions, to move the bill speedily through, so that we can rightly—rightly—
celebrate in 2015.
I think it is important, too, to note that the role of the Gove rnor-General—and I say
this as someone who is quite interested in things constitutional—is actually incredibly
important and an essential part of New Zealand’s constitutional and democratic
structure. Orders in Council are not unusua l, and I think it is difficult to start
scaremongering around that point. I just want to highlight that.
But I want to return to the importance of the national memorial. In 2015 we will
remember that 100 years ago Kiwis and Australians landed on the shores of Gallipoli,
and that they gave their lives. The very least we can do here tonight is to move this bill
through, simply, gently, and kindly—

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: With dignity.
SIMON O’CONNOR : —with dignity, and in a way that was not accorded—
[Interruption]; as we are now hearing from th e Opposition—to our men who landed on
those shores. In 2015 we will remember them, and tonight we begin that process. Again,
it is lamentable that in doing so we ha ve, I think, brought some dishonour amongst
them. But I hope that, on finishing this sp eech tonight, we return some honour to those
men, to those fallen, and that all of us here in this House will unite to celebrate in 2015
the building of this national park.
4824 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 28 Aug 2012

and (c).
Motion agreed to.
TAXATION (ANNUAL RATES, RETURNS FILING, AND REMEDIAL
MATTERS) BILL
In Committee
Part 1  Annual rates of income tax

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: I am very pleased to be able to
take a call on Part 1 of the Taxation (Annua l Rates, Returns Filing, and Remedial
Matters) Bill, where we are being asked—

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Not as pleased as the chairman.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: —to confirm the annual rates of income tax, and I hope it also
pleases the chairman that I take a call at th is stage. The rates of income tax are very
critical to outcomes in our society, and I want to put firmly my view that this part of the
bill is one of the ones that we struggle with  the most. We will support the broader bill,
but I would like to have a qu ick look at the outcomes that can be attributed to the
current rates of income tax, and ask the Mi nister of Revenue why we should confirm
these particular sets of tax rates now.
Recent reports have indicated pretty clearly that we are doing poorly as a society. We
are becoming more and more unequal. A good d eal of this inequality in our society
comes as a direct result of the so-called tax switch in 2010. And we know that in that
tax switch 44 percent of the value of the tax cuts that National gave out went to the top
10 percent of earners, and just 2 percent of the value of those tax cuts went to the
bottom 20 percent of earners in New Zealand. That tax switch benefited greatly those at
the top—some pocketing an extra $1,000 a w eek—while those at the bottom very
quickly had any tax cut gobbled up in GST.
There have been reports in recent days and w eeks that indicate that the effects of the
current tax rates are disastrous—increasingly disastrous. In fact, they were labelled
quite accurately by the leader of the Labour Party as a bloody disgrace. Firstly, I want to
look at The Netherlands Study , commissioned by Every Child Counts, which came out
on the 22nd of this month. It indicated very clearly that we need to invest in policies that
support children and parents, and ensure that they have the right tools and support, if we
want to eradicate poverty in this country. A nd all the evidence show s, according to the
28 Aug 2012 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc) Bill 4825
report, that poor outcomes for kids in poverty cost taxpay ers a good deal, and that is
estimated at between $6 billion and $8 billion a year. New Zealand spends around a
third less each year than the Nordic countries  on this. The Netherlands spends less than
half, but continues to achieve excellent outcomes. That is the first report.
The next report that we have had recently was the Household incomes in New
Zealand report, which indicated that inequaliti es in New Zealand are worse than ever.
The median income across all households  fell by 3 percent between 2009 and 2011.
That follows 15 years of steady growth in those median incomes. We also know that
without Working for Families, a Labour policy, things would be a lot worse in terms of
that inequality in our country, and the outcomes for our citizens in poverty would be a
lot better if we had both Working for Families and a fairer set of tax policies.
The fall of 3 percent in real terms in the income of those people on the median wage
is one thing, but we also know that the same thing led to an effect where the proportion
of kids in poverty in New Zealand has gone  from 15 percent to 21 percent between
2007 and 2011. This is through po licies that can be tied back  to a number of things,
including things like health care and other proactive measures , but also very firmly tied
back, actually, to particular tax choices that we make.
We are being asked here, I remind the Comm ittee, to affirm the annual rates of
income tax in Part 1. We are being asked to say that the current set of policies the
Government has in the tax area are fair and are leading to positive outcomes for our
citizens. I wish to argue that they are not.
The Children’s Commissioner’s report is the third of these reports that has come out
recently that points to very unequal outcome s that I wish to draw attention to. It
indicates a 25 percent incidence of child poverty—270,000 child ren in poverty. The
costs of a poor start,  as we have said, amount to ar ound $6 billion fo r those children
living in poverty, which we pick up as taxpayers every year. So I want to argue that this
particular set of tax rates benefits the wealthiest in our society in the short term, but is
actually bad for all of us in the long term as it leads to disinvestment in social goods,
and also disinvestment in those things th at are good for all of us in the economy,
including public services, and the right incentives, as I said, to grow our economy.
We have also learnt in recent days that 90 of the 100 wealthiest New Zealanders are
not on the top tax rate—90 of the 100 wealthiest New Zeala nders are not on the top tax
rate—and that, in fact, a full 50 percent of those with wealth over $50 million are not on
the top tax rate in New Zeala nd. They are able to structure their affairs in such a way
that they do not pay their fair share of tax. Labour stands for fair taxes in a fair
economy, and we would impose a capital gains tax that would make sure that people did
not avoid paying the tax that they are due to pay, that they would carry their fair share in
terms of taxation, but also that a neutral signal is se nt to the investors in respect of the
productive sector. When people invest their money, they make a choice about whether it
is better for them to invest in productive assets, which are good, in fact, for all of New
Zealand in terms of exports, or to choose, as they currently ofte n do, to put money into
the housing sector, where the returns are artific ially distorted by the absence of a capital
gains tax.
There are only three countries in the OECD that do not currently have a capital gains
tax. This Government is choosing not to pu t one in. We are told—the rumour is—that
that is because the current tax capabilities in  the department are not up to scratch. The
computer system could not handle a capital gains tax, and that is one reason why the
Government cannot go near it. Mr Key has pointed to that in a Valentine’s Day promise.
He talked about $1 billion that needed to be spent to remedy this problem. That does not
seem to have been spent. We have no ti metable, no understanding of when our tax
system will be able to handle the changes that we need as a country. In fact, we are left
4826 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc) Bill 28 Aug 2012
confirming current policies, by and large, because our tax computing system will not
handle the big changes that New Zealand needs to grow its economy, to be an effective
country in terms of addressing the issues of poverty, and also to make sure that
businesses have the environment they need to  grow exports. Instead, what we are faced
with is a growing balance of  trade deficits and children increasingly living in poverty.
The largest gap between rich and poor that New Zealand has ever had on record is what
we are faced with this week.
It is a bloody disgrace. David Shearer is ri ght. We need to address these things. We
need a fairer tax system wher e all New Zealanders know that if they put their shoulder
to the wheel, they can get ahead, they can contribute, they can put food on the table for
their families that is nutritious and healthy,  and they can afford to buy the shoes they
need for school, the raincoats, the textbooks, and all the other things that are necessary
for kids to succeed and not feel like society is against them.
I put it to you that this current annual rates of income tax confirmation should be
thoroughly questioned by all sides of the Committee, because in so far as National has a
plan to address these issues of poverty—

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: We have a plan. We have a plan.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: —and inequality, it is not wo rking. We have heard of 120-
point plans. We do not actuall y see any plans with measurab le targets. As Mr McClay
points out, they say that th ey have a plan, but we do not see any with measurable
targets, and we certainly do not see any targets being achieved. The real economy is
smaller now than it was when National ca me here. The only thing that keeps the
economy growing is population growth. Real wa ges are lower than they were in 2008.
The median wage, we have learnt, is dow n 3 percent, and peopl e are suffering. This
Government is not delivering the brighter futu re that was promised. It is delivering a
poor shadow of that, and New Zealanders ar e tiring of it. They wish for stronger tax
policy that would address thes e inequities, and instead we are asked to confirm the
status quo. I put it to you that that is not an adequate solution. Thank you.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: I have just said to my colleague beside me,
the senior Government whip Michael Woodhou se, to wake up. You are not allowed to
sleep in this House. He said that it was not his fault—he had lis tened to the beginning,
the middle, and the end of the speech from the last member, David Clark. How is it that
two MPs from Dunedin, one from Dunedin North and another MP representing Dunedin
South, can have such a different grasp of real ity when it comes to issues as important to
New Zealanders as this? One is grounded in reality, and one in the area of fanciful land,
and, of course, it is Mr Woodhouse who has his feet firmly on the ground.
What we heard from the last speaker in this debate was wishful thinking. The one
point that I take from what Mr Clark said was to impose more tax. He said: “Impose
more tax.” He said that David Shearer is right; impose more tax. Well, he is actually not
right, he is left, but he is so much further le ft than what people in this country want at
this time that it concerns me greatly for members opposite, who believe that their leader
is right. Impose more tax on New Zealanders.
We heard about a capital gains tax—capit al gains tax. We heard about it again,
recycled from the last election—a capital gains tax on all businesses and farms, on all
houses, on beach houses, on everything that Ne w Zealanders own. Those members will
stand up in this Chamber and say: “No, no. That  wasn’t what we meant before the last
election. Indeed, we had a good plan before th e last election and New Zealanders just
didn’t understand it.” We hear that from the Labour Opposition all the time. I would say
that not only did New Zealanders understand, but they rejected imposing more tax, they
rejected an unfair capital gains tax, and they elected the policy that is before us,
delivered by the honourable Minister in the chair, the Minister of Revenue.
28 Aug 2012 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc) Bill 4827
The Finance and Expenditure Committee ha d an opportunity to hear from all New
Zealanders on this piece of legislation, the Taxation (Annua l Rates, Returns Filing, and
Remedial Matters) Bill, and on Part 1, and we took extra time, as we often do in the
Finance and Expenditure Committee, to lis ten to those submitters on their views.
Although there were a range of views, I believe  that the bill that has been brought back
to this Committee clearly follows the views of those whom we heard from, from all
around New Zealand. Those views were simp le. They were that David Shearer is
wrong—do not impose more unnecessary tax, we do not want a capital gains tax; it will
penalise us. We want a tax sy stem that will benefit New Ze alanders, and give them an
opportunity to invest in them selves and go forward. I comme nd this wonderful piece of
legislation that the Minister of Revenue has brought to the House.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call on
this Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing, and Remedial Matters) Bill—they always
have such exciting titles. It is, of course, instructive to listen to the speech of the
member who has just resumed his seat, T odd McClay, because he finished off by
making a monumental blunder, which was to say that because Labour might be
considering some new forms of taxation to  neutralise investment  signals across the
economy—a very good thing, any economis t would say—he is leaping to the
conclusion that that would therefore mean a higher net tax burden. In fact, that is not
necessarily the case, as it was not the cas e that the Government’s own tax switch was
not tax neutral, but $1 billion in  the red over 4 years. That is  leaving aside the fact that
upper-income earners, of course, got a massive tax windfall, and medium-wage earners,
just for example, have gone backwards, because  their real wages, even before tax, are 3
percent lower today than they were when the current Government took office.
Looking at the title of this bill, and l ooking at Maggie Barry opposite and thinking
about annuals and perennials, I am reminded that although the rates revision is an
annual gardening term, the Minister in the ch air is in fact a perennial Minister of
Revenue. In fact, so perennial is the Mi nister that he is now amending his own
amendments to his own bills on previous am endments from previous Governments. A
bit like the perennial spinach that keeps pe ople fed with greens dur ing the winter, there
is the perennial—I think you would say he is  a spinach-type of Minister. There is no
icing on that cake—well, maybe there is, actually. He is more a meat-and-potatoes man,
is he not?
In all seriousness, this seemingly innocuous bill does give the Labour Party some
delicious opportunities to remind the good pe ople of New Zealand, for whom we are
working so hard, that we had some excelle nt policies for them that they narrowly—
narrowly—failed to grasp at the last election, some of which are still going to occupy an
important place in their futures. For example, there is KiwiSaver. This bill tinkers with
KiwiSaver. National’s big, bad savings secret was—wait for it—first off, it reduced the
member contribution rate from 4 percent to 2 percent. That was brave—that was brave.
Now it is putting it up by precisely half the amount that it put it down last time—stirring
stuff from the National Government! It half re-amended its own amendments.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: It’s time for another shave. Ring the bell.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Would the member for Rotorua like to consider that one
in relative silence? That woul d be lovely. The really importa nt thing about this is that
Labour’s universal KiwiSaver plan achieve d the objective of growing New Zealand’s
savings rate by—wait for it—four times the rate  of National’s tepid plan, part of which
we are rather sadly and forlor nly debating tonight. That is  four times more opportunity
for New Zealand mums and dads to save for their future and to build up a nest egg. For
somebody who starts out in work in their mi d-20s and saves at the minimum wage, that
was going to be at least half a million dollars by the time they hit 65—a really important
4828 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc) Bill 28 Aug 2012
complement to their superannuation and a r eal opportunity to get a deposit on a house,
to have a nest egg, and to buffer them from major ill fortune. But remember that
Labour’s savings plan would have had a rate of savings increase four times faster than
this tepid little amendment in this bill.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Four times?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Four times—Kiwis would be four times better off under
Labour’s plan than under this so qualified little change, which only half reverses the
previous backsliding.
Then, of course, we get on to the subject of GST. There are GST amendments in this
bill. Well, go ahead, make our day. New Zealanders are not going to forget that GST
has been raised by this Government on ev ery single New Zealand family and on every
single product: the school books, the shoes,  the raincoats, th e milk, the bread—you
name it, GST on these has all gone up to 15 percent. Kiwis cannot afford that—they
cannot afford that. That was why Labour offered some relief in that area in the last—

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I cannot let the moment go without
injecting a note of reality into this debate on the Ta xation (Annual Rates, Returns
Filing, and Remedial Matters) Bill. The previous speaker, David Cunliffe, has waxed
lyrical about KiwiSaver.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: That wasn’t lyrical; that was prosaic. I waxed prosaic.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Well, he attempted to be lyrical. It certainly was very
Harvardian prosaic, shall we say. The point I wa nt to make is simply this: the allegation
put forward is that enrolments in the KiwiSaver scheme have somehow stalled since this
Government came to office. I was there, as the member acknowledges, when the
KiwiSaver scheme was devised, and I should tell the Committee that in its original
conception the plan was that we would hit—wait for it—700,000 KiwiSavers by 2015.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: How many are there?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Seven hundred thousand by 2015. In February 2009, we
topped a million.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: That’s because it was a good idea.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: And the member opposite says  it was a good idea. The
members opposite are arguing, if they would just  bear with me for a moment, that the
steps this Government has taken have been to  the detraction of KiwiSaver. As I say, we
have topped a million KiwiSavers in February 2009. A little over 2½ years later, we are
within days of hitting 2 million. The point I wa nt to make to the Committee is that if
this scheme has been so tarnished, so ti nkered with, and so destroyed, how come we
have doubled its membership in 2½ years? I would have thought that had the claims the
member was making had validity, we would ha ve seen a downward tail, but, in fact,
here we are going to be by the end of 2012 not at 700,000 but probably three times that
original prediction, and twice what we were early in 2009.
I listened to the previous speaker bar Mr Cunliffe, Dr David Cl ark, and Mr Cunliffe
as well talk about the Labour Party’s taxation plans, and I listened in vain. What I heard
from both was a lament about current circum stances, the fact that  incomes have fallen,
with no reference to the global financial crisis, the biggest crisis to hit the world since
the Great Depression—no reference to that. An d then I heard two suggestions made as
to what we could do to rectify the situation. One was to bring in a capital gains tax. That
was rejected by the electorate last year. It ha s been rejected by the electorate every time
a political party has campaigned on it at every election over the last 30 to 40 years. It
was also rejected substan tially by the Tax Working Group in its work in 2009-10. But
the Labour Party clings to it, and when it real ises it will not work, it then falls back on
the claim that the only reason we do not have it is because the Inland Revenue
Department’s computer will not let us design one. The reality is th at we are about to
28 Aug 2012 Taxation (Annual Rates, Returns Filing etc) Bill 4829
embark on the biggest re-design of our technology since the introduction of the first
system in 1991, and we will be making announcements about that and the scope of it a
little later in the year.

items.speaker: So we are left with this
items.text: a lament from the Opposition about the annual tax rates and
a failed plea that the overall solution lies in a capital gains tax. Then Dr Clark made the
point that low-income people and middle-inco me people have been the big losers from

were on changes to the bottom two steps. I do not think the Labour Party opposes the
reduction in the bottom two steps of taxation, which was where the bulk of the spending
occurred. So what we come down to is this: the one thing that they have not said tonight
is that their bold new plan is to put the top tax rate back up. What happened the last time
they did that, in 1999, was that we saw a massive explosion in the number of trusts—we
saw a massive explosion post-1999 in the num ber of trusts—and ta x avoidance and tax
evasion, and one of the reasons why we delib erately aligned the trust and the personal
rates in 2010 was to stop—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Who was the Minister of Revenue?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Michael Cullen. The reason we  deliberately aligned those
rates was to stop that process—[Bell rung] Mr Chair—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Chairperson. I seek to raise a point

that the Minister has resumed his seat—

order is.

on for 5 minutes suggesting that I had alleged that KiwiSaver was in decline—

items.text: Mr Chairman.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Mr Chair.

items.text: I will hear the Minister, who—

items.text: He sought the call, and I had given him the call.
You raised the point of order, and I am now referring back to the call.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairpers on. Without wishing to
second-guess a call that has already been given, you will remember that I was seeking a
